html:
A great carved basalt disc from Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, about 3.6 metres across and weighing some 24 tonnes. It was likely carved in the early 1500s, under Moctezuma II or just before him, and is the best known work of Mexica sculpture.

Despite its popular name, it is not a working calendar. It shows the Mexica view of time. In the centre is a face, usually read as the sun god Tonatiuh or the earth monster. Around it are four squares for the four earlier ages, or "suns", each destroyed in turn. The ring beyond holds the 20 day signs of the ritual calendar, and two fire serpents circle the edge. It may have been used as an altar or a stone for sacrifice.

After the conquest the Spanish buried it in the main square of Mexico City. It was dug up in 1790, during work near the cathedral, and is now in the National Museum of Anthropology, a symbol of Mexico.
